summary.headline: Benchmark comparison passed with caveats. On the finest mesh (256×256 cells) the velocity profiles match Ghia et al. (1982) to within \(0.0092\,U\) and the vortex strength to \(0.077\,\%\).

findings: Velocity profiles (a, b). On the finest mesh every benchmark point is matched to within \(0.0092\,U\) (tolerance \(0.005\,U\)); the typical (RMS) difference is \(0.0025\,U\) for \(u\) and \(0.0051\,U\) for \(v\).
Return flow (c). \(u_{\min} = -0.21399\,U\) versus \(-0.2109\,U\) in the benchmark; its position differs by \(0.64\) benchmark grid spacings, i.e. within the benchmark's resolution.
Vortex (d). Strength \(\psi_{\min} = -0.1035\,UL\), \(0.077\,\%\) from the benchmark; the centre is \(0.42\) benchmark grid spacings from Ghia's.

Mesh convergence. The answers change by a factor of about \(4.2\) less with each halving of the cells (observed order \(p \approx 2.1\) for the \(u\) profile, design order 2). The finest-mesh uncertainty (GCI) of \(\psi_{\min}\) is \(0.021\,\%\).

Converged and conserving mass. All runs stopped on their residual targets, the probed velocities changed by at most \(1.8 \times 10^{-8}\,U\) over the last 10 % of iterations, and the net flow through the vertical centreline is \(\le 2.9 \times 10^{-5}\,UL\) (must be 0).
Caveat: (b) v-profile: max difference from Ghia \(0.0092\,U\) above \(0.005\,U\).
Caveat: \(y_c\): observed order \(0.844\) outside \(1 \le p \le 3\) (change between the two finest meshes only \(6.3 \times 10^{-6}\), GCI \(0.0013\,\%\)).
limitations: The benchmark is itself a numerical solution on a 129×129 grid, not an experiment: agreement shows that the equations are solved correctly, not that a real cavity (3D, finite length, rounded corners) behaves this way.
Ghia's locations are grid points \(h_G = 1/128\) apart, so location differences below about one spacing cannot be resolved.
Velocities near the two top corners (singular) were not compared; the benchmark tables do not cover them.

problem.description: A square cavity full of fluid is driven by its sliding top wall (the lid). Find the steady flow inside the cavity and compare it with the published benchmark solution of Ghia, Ghia & Shin (1982).
setup: Square cavity of side \(L\), completely filled with an incompressible Newtonian fluid.
The top wall (the lid) slides to the right at constant speed \(U\); the other three walls are stationary. All walls are no-slip.
The cavity is very long in the third direction, so the flow is two-dimensional.
Positions are scaled by \(L\), velocities by \(U\) and the stream function by \(U L\), as in the benchmark.

wanted.text: Horizontal velocity \(u\) along the vertical centreline \(x = L/2\), compared with Ghia Table I
Vertical velocity \(v\) along the horizontal centreline \(y = L/2\), compared with Ghia Table II
Strongest return flow: minimum of \(u\) on the vertical centreline, and where it occurs
Centre of the primary vortex \((x, y)\) and its strength (minimum stream function)

problem.reference: Ghia, Ghia & Shin (1982), J. Comput. Phys. 48, 387-411: benchmark numerical solution (129 x 129 grid), Table I (u), Table II (v), Table V (vortex properties), read from reference/ghia1982_re100.yaml.

rows.name: Two-dimensional flow
rows.check: The cavity is very long in \(z\) (given), so nothing varies along it. Imposed with one cell and empty front/back patches. Real cavities of finite length have 3D end-wall effects.

rows.name: Steady, laminar flow
rows.check: \(Re = UL/\nu = 100\). At this Reynolds number the cavity flow is a single steady vortex; the benchmark is a steady laminar solution at the same \(Re\). Steadiness of the computed state is checked (Run health): the probed velocities stop changing.

rows.name: Incompressible (constant density)
rows.check: \(Ma = U/c \le 1/300 = 0.0033 \ll 0.3\). The fluid is not named, so the speed of sound \(c\) is bounded from below by 300 m/s (slower than sound in air or any common liquid; approximate value).

rows.name: Newtonian fluid, constant viscosity
rows.check: Given ("incompressible Newtonian fluid"); isothermal, so \(\nu\) is constant.

rows.name: Gravity does not affect the flow
rows.check: Constant density: gravity only adds a hydrostatic pressure, which does not move the fluid.

rows.name: No slip on all walls; ideal sharp lid corners
rows.check: The fluid moves with each wall. The velocity jump at the two top corners is kept as in the benchmark; it makes the corner flow singular (Theory, step 3).

theory.intro: The cavity flow has no exact solution: the convection term makes the equations nonlinear. The comparison therefore uses the benchmark of Ghia et al. Theory still fixes what the answer depends on (one number, \(Re\)), what must hold exactly (no net flow through any line across the cavity), and the expected shape of the flow. The algebraic steps marked below are checked by SymPy.

steps.label: Governing equations: continuity and momentum for a steady, incompressible, Newtonian fluid
steps.note: Mass is conserved, and each fluid parcel's momentum changes only through pressure and viscous forces. The left side (convection) makes the equations nonlinear: no exact solution is known.

steps.label: Scaling: measure lengths in L, velocities in U, pressure in ρU²
steps.note: One number, Re, decides the shape of the flow (checked by SymPy below). This is why the benchmark reports x/L, u/U and ψ/(UL): those are the same for every cavity at Re = 100.

steps.label: Boundary conditions (no slip)
steps.latex: \mathbf{u} = (U, 0)\ \text{on the lid } (y = L),\qquad \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\ \text{on the other three walls}
steps.note: At the two top corners the wall velocity jumps from U to 0. There the velocity gradient is infinite (a corner singularity), so local errors near those corners shrink slowly with refinement in every method, including the benchmark.

steps.label: Stream function: the requested measure of the vortex
steps.latex: u = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y},\quad v = -\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x},\qquad \psi = 0 \text{ on all walls},\qquad \int_0^L u(x, y)\,dy = 0
steps.note: Lines of constant ψ are streamlines, and the difference of ψ between two points is the flow rate between them. The walls are one streamline (ψ = 0). The lid drags the fluid clockwise, so ψ < 0 inside; its minimum marks the vortex centre and |ψ_min| is the flow rate circulating around it. Because no fluid crosses the walls, the net flow through any vertical line is zero: the forward flow under the lid is exactly returned lower down. This is a check on the simulation.

steps.label: What else theory predicts (without numbers)
steps.latex: Re \to 0:\ \text{flow symmetric about } x = L/2;\qquad Re > 0:\ \text{vortex shifted towards the lid's downstream side } (x > L/2)
steps.note: Slow (Stokes) flow is reversible, so its pattern is mirror-symmetric about the vertical centreline. Inertia carries momentum in the lid direction and breaks that symmetry. Viscous-flow theory (Moffatt 1964, J. Fluid Mech. 18) also predicts small counter-rotating eddies in the bottom corners, with ψ > 0; the benchmark's Table V lists two of them (not requested here).

derived.label: Reynolds number
derived.why: The only parameter of the dimensionless problem (Step 2): it compares the fluid's inertia, which carries momentum around the cavity, with viscous friction, which spreads it out. Two cavities with the same \(Re\) have the same flow pattern. The benchmark column used is the one for this \(Re\).

derived.label: Lid transit time
derived.why: Time for the lid to move one cavity width. Flow features are carried around the cavity on this time scale.

derived.label: Viscous diffusion time
derived.why: Time for friction to spread momentum across the cavity. Its ratio to the transit time is \(Re\): here momentum is carried around faster than it diffuses, so the vortex is pushed off-centre.

derived.label: Cell Péclet number, coarsest mesh
derived.why: Convection versus diffusion across ONE cell, at the lid speed. Above about 2, central differencing of the convection term can produce wiggles; this is why a linear-upwind (upwind-biased, still second order) scheme was chosen (Decisions).

params.meaning: cell size of the coarsest mesh, \(L/32\)

derived.label: Cell Péclet number, finest mesh
derived.why: On the finest mesh diffusion dominates within each cell, so any scheme behaves well there.

params.meaning: cell size of the finest mesh, \(L/256\)

derived.label: Benchmark grid spacing
derived.why: Ghia et al. stored their solution only at grid points this far apart, so their vortex-centre coordinates and the location of the velocity minimum are known only to within about one spacing. Location differences smaller than this cannot be judged.

params.meaning: number of grid intervals per side in the benchmark (129 grid points)

self_checks.name: dimensionless momentum equation contains only \(1/Re\), with \(Re = UL/\nu\)
\(\int_0^L u\,dy = \psi(x, L) - \psi(x, 0)\), which is 0 because \(\psi = 0\) on every wall

decisions.choice: Steady, incompressible, laminar, Newtonian flow with \(\nu = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\)
decisions.why: \(Re = UL/\nu = 100\): the cavity flow is steady and laminar at this Reynolds number (the benchmark itself is a steady laminar solution). The given viscosity is used directly; only \(\nu\) matters for incompressible flow, not the density.
decisions.affects: Defines the equations solved. A turbulence model would add viscosity that does not exist.
decisions.alternatives: A transient laminar solver run until the flow stops changing (same answer, slower).

decisions.choice: simpleFoam: steady incompressible solver (SIMPLE family), started from the icoFoam/cavity tutorial geometry
decisions.why: The problem asks for the steady flow; a steady solver goes there directly instead of following the physical start-up. The closest tutorial (icoFoam/cavity) is transient and at \(Re = 10\); its geometry, patch names and boundary conditions were kept.
decisions.affects: None on the converged answer if the steady solution is unique and stable (true at \(Re = 100\)); it decides only how the answer is reached.
decisions.alternatives: icoFoam or pimpleFoam run to steady state: they must follow the whole physical start-up (many lid transit times \(L/U\)) with a time step limited by the Courant number on the finest mesh, which is much slower.

decisions.choice: Square \(L \times L\) cavity, one cell thick in \(z\) with empty front and back (2D)
decisions.why: The cavity is very long in \(z\), so the flow is 2D; empty patches make OpenFOAM solve the 2D equations. Origin at the bottom-left corner as in Ghia et al.
decisions.affects: Geometry exactly as in the problem; 3D end-wall effects are excluded by construction.
decisions.alternatives: A 3D cavity with end walls (a different problem; the benchmark is 2D).

decisions.choice: Lid: \(\mathbf{u} = (U, 0)\) on the top wall; no slip \(\mathbf{u} = 0\) on the other three walls; pressure zero-gradient on all walls
decisions.why: The fluid sticks to each wall (no slip), so it moves with the lid at the top and is at rest at the fixed walls. Zero-gradient pressure is the standard partner of a fixed velocity at a wall.
decisions.affects: Defines the problem. The two top corners carry a velocity jump (from \(U\) to 0), a singularity shared with the benchmark.
decisions.alternatives: Regularised lid velocity that falls smoothly to zero at the corners: a different problem from the benchmark.

decisions.choice: Initial state: fluid at rest, \(\mathbf{u} = 0,\ p = 0\); pressure fixed to 0 in cell 0 (pRefCell 0, pRefValue 0)
decisions.why: A steady solution does not depend on the starting guess. In a closed cavity only pressure differences are defined, so one cell must fix the pressure level.
decisions.affects: None on velocities or on the stream function; it sets only the (arbitrary) pressure level.
decisions.alternatives: Starting from a coarse-mesh solution (faster on fine meshes, but couples the runs).

decisions.why: Four meshes with ratio 2 give two independent estimates of the observed order of accuracy and allow Richardson extrapolation and a GCI from the three finest. The finest (256) is twice as fine as the benchmark grid (128 intervals). Uniform cells keep the order-of-accuracy test clean.
decisions.affects: Discretisation error; measured in the Comparison section.
decisions.alternatives: Cells clustered towards the walls (grading): more accurate in the wall layers for the same cell count, but complicates Richardson extrapolation.

decisions.choice: Second-order schemes: bounded Gauss linearUpwind grad(U) for convection; Gauss linear gradients; Gauss linear corrected Laplacian; linear interpolation
decisions.why: Convection matters at \(Re = 100\), so its scheme sets the accuracy. Linear-upwind is second order and stays well behaved on the coarsest mesh, where the cell Péclet number \(U h/\nu\) exceeds 2 and pure central differencing can wiggle. bounded removes the \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}\) part that is non-zero before convergence (standard for steady solvers). The mesh is orthogonal, so corrected adds nothing.
decisions.affects: Order of accuracy (expected 2) and the size of the mesh error.
decisions.alternatives: First-order upwind (robust but adds numerical viscosity, roughly an error of order \(Uh/2\) in \(\nu\)); central Gauss linear (second order, can oscillate at cell Péclet > 2).

decisions.choice: SIMPLEC (consistent yes), velocity relaxed by 0.9, pressure not relaxed
decisions.why: The momentum equation is nonlinear (convection), so the velocity update must be damped. SIMPLEC tolerates weak damping (0.9) without pressure relaxation, which converges much faster than plain SIMPLE (U 0.7, p 0.3). Orthogonal mesh: no non-orthogonal correctors needed.
decisions.affects: Only how quickly the answer is reached, provided the run is converged.
decisions.alternatives: Plain SIMPLE with U 0.7 / p 0.3 (slower); a transient solver (see Solver).

decisions.choice: GAMG (multigrid) for \(p\), each solve reducing its residual 20-fold (relTol 0.05); Gauss–Seidel smoother for \(\mathbf{u}\) (relTol 0.1)
decisions.why: Each SIMPLE iteration only needs an improved, not an exact, pressure; the outer iterations remove what is left. Multigrid handles the domain-wide pressure field efficiently on fine meshes.
decisions.affects: Speed only; the converged answer does not depend on these once the outer iterations converge.
decisions.alternatives: PCG/DIC for \(p\) (as in the tutorial; slower on fine meshes); tighter relTol (more work per iteration).

decisions.choice: Stop when the normalised residuals fall below \(10^{-11}\) (velocity) and \(10^{-10}\) (pressure), cap of 20 000 iterations; fields written every 1000 iterations with 12 significant digits
decisions.why: Residuals here are meaningful (no field is zero), but they are only a proxy. Convergence is confirmed physically: the probed velocities must stop changing (see Run health). 12 digits keep round-off out of the error analysis.
decisions.affects: Iteration error (made negligible against the mesh error) and output precision.
decisions.alternatives: A fixed iteration count (wasteful on coarse meshes, possibly too short on fine ones).

decisions.choice: Probes of \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(p\) at four interior points, every iteration
decisions.why: The physical steadiness check: these velocities must stop changing. Centreline profiles and the stream function are computed afterwards from the cell-centre velocities (by cell index, never by exact coordinates); OpenFOAM's streamFunction utility is used as an independent cross-check of the vortex strength.
decisions.affects: How convergence is judged and how the requested quantities are measured.
decisions.alternatives: OpenFOAM line sampling (sets) at the benchmark points: equivalent, but interpolates with its own scheme.

preflight.purpose: Before the production runs, short runs on the coarsest and finest meshes check that the setup runs, stays stable and converges, and estimate the run time. A failure here stops the workflow before any long run.

preflight.conclusion: All pre-flight checks passed; residuals fall steadily on both meshes. The projected length of the finest run (≈ 3948 iterations) was a lower bound: it actually needed 10864 iterations (679 s), still well within the 15-minute budget.

model.real: Square cavity, side \(L = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}\), very long in \(z\)
model.model: The same square, one cell thick in \(z\) with empty front and back: OpenFOAM solves the 2D equations.
Fixed velocity \((U, 0, 0)\) on the top boundary; the corners are left sharp.
Kinematic pressure \(p/\rho\) and \(\nu\); density never needed. \(Re = 100\) as in the benchmark.

model.real: The flow after all start-up motion has died out
model.model: Solved directly with the steady SIMPLEC algorithm; each iteration is a step towards the steady solution, not a step in time.

model.real: Velocities on the centrelines, vortex centre and strength
model.model: Centreline values: mean of the two cell columns (rows) beside the centreline, interpolated to the benchmark points with a cubic spline. Stream function: OpenFOAM's streamFunction (from the face fluxes), minimum refined with a bicubic spline.

meshes.intro: The same problem is solved on 4 uniform meshes. Each has cells half the size of the previous one, so the change in the answer measures the error caused by the mesh. The benchmark used a grid \(h_G = 1/128\).

notes: A residual measures how far the current iterate is from satisfying the discretised equations (normalised, so it is a relative measure). Runs stop when it falls below \(1 \times 10^{-11}\) for \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) for \(p\).

Physical check: the velocity at four probe points must change by less than \(1 \times 10^{-7}\,U\) over the last 10 % of iterations, far below the mesh error. Two earlier attempts with looser residual targets failed this check, first on the 128² mesh and then on the 256² mesh (Insights); each time the residual targets were tightened and all meshes re-run, never the check.
Continuity error: OpenFOAM's 'sum local' mass error of the last iteration.
Log checks: no crash, no NaN, no growing residuals (automatic, cfdlib.monitor).
Iterations grow about 3.6× per refinement: SIMPLE removes cavity-wide errors slowly on fine meshes.

comparison.kind: Benchmark: the simulation is compared with a trusted, very fine numerical solution of the same equations (Ghia, Ghia & Shin (1982), J. Comput. Phys. 48, 387-411). Differences are in units of the lid speed \(U\) and the cavity side \(L\); locations also in benchmark grid spacings \(h_G\).

definitions.name: Largest profile difference
definitions.meaning: Worst case over the 15 (Table I) or 15 (Table II) interior benchmark points; the wall points are boundary conditions and are left out.

definitions.name: RMS profile difference
definitions.meaning: Typical difference over the same points.

definitions.name: Observed order and Richardson extrapolation
definitions.latex: p = \frac{\ln\left|\frac{f_1 - f_2}{f_2 - f_3}\right|}{\ln 2},\qquad f_{\mathrm{ext}} = f_3 + \frac{f_3 - f_2}{2^p - 1}
definitions.meaning: From three meshes (1 coarse, 3 fine): how fast the answer settles, and the value it settles to (the zero-cell-size estimate). Profiles use one order from the RMS change between meshes.

definitions.name: Grid Convergence Index (GCI)
definitions.meaning: A conservative band for the mesh error of the finest result (Celik et al. 2008).

findings: The remaining difference is not mesh error. Extrapolating to zero cell size changes the comparison little: the extrapolated profiles still differ from Ghia by up to \(0.005\,U\) (\(u\)) and \(0.0092\,U\) (\(v\)), while the uncertainty bands of the finest mesh are at most \(1.3 \times 10^{-4}\,U\). The gap is therefore not mesh error of this simulation. Its most likely source is the benchmark's own discretisation error (its grid, \(h_G = 1/128\), is coarser than the finest mesh here); the supplied data cannot prove this, and a second, independent benchmark would settle it. Until then the benchmark should be read as accurate to about this level, not to its printed digits.

Not a scheme artefact. The 128² case was re-run with central differencing for convection (Gauss linear) instead of linear-upwind. The two answers differ by at most \(1.9 \times 10^{-4}\,U\) at the benchmark points (and \(0.028\,\%\) in \(\psi_{\min}\)), while both differ from Ghia by up to \(0.0093\,U\). The scheme changes the answer far less than the gap to the benchmark, so that gap is not caused by the choice of convection scheme.

Where the differences are largest. In the thin layer under the lid, where \(u\) falls from \(U\) to the return flow over a few percent of the cavity (Figure 4, right panel), and near the downstream wall for \(v\). These are the regions of steepest gradients, next to the singular corners.

Physics check. The vortex centre lies \(0.12\,L\) right of the centreline and above mid-height: inertia carries the fluid towards the downstream wall before it turns down, as Theory predicted (a slow, inertia-free flow would be symmetric).

Two independent stream functions agree. \(\psi_{\min}\) from OpenFOAM's flux-based streamFunction and from integrating the cell velocities differ by \(8.7 \times 10^{-9}\) (relative) on the finest mesh.

Mass check, honestly. The check fixed before the runs ("\(|\psi|\) on the lid below \(1 \times 10^{-4}\)") failed with the velocity-integrated stream function (\(3.7 \times 10^{-4}\,UL\) on the finest mesh, concentrated in the last cell next to the top-right corner) but is exactly zero with OpenFOAM's flux-based one. It tested the post-processing at the singular corner, not mass conservation, so it was replaced by the net flow through the vertical centreline (see Insights).

insights.problem: The first wsl ... -- bash /mnt/d/.../probe.sh call failed with "No such file or directory: C:/Program Files/Git/mnt/d/...", and a later call made grep report "Binary file (standard input) matches" instead of printing.
insights.diagnosis: The agent's shell tool on this machine is Git Bash (MSYS), not PowerShell. MSYS rewrites any argument that looks like a POSIX path (/mnt/d/...) into a Windows path before WSL sees it. Separately, wsl.exe prints its own warning in UTF-16, so the output contains NUL bytes.
insights.fix: Prefix the call with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 and pipe the output through tr -d "\000".
insights.lesson: environment.md only describes PowerShell quoting; the Git Bash path conversion is a second, different trap on the same machine.
insights.guideline: environment.md: add a "From Git Bash" block: MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04 --cd "/mnt/d/Projects/Agentic CFD" -- /home/tomyud/venvs/cfd/bin/python -m ..., and note the NUL bytes in wsl.exe output.

insights.problem: SKILL.md says "run python -m cfdlib.contract early to see uncovered settings", but the CLI needs a results.json, which does not exist during setup.
insights.diagnosis: The contract CLI checks a whole report; the decisions-coverage part (contract.uncovered_settings) is only reachable from Python.
insights.fix: A 15-line case-local script (scratch/check_decisions.py) renders the template once and calls contract.uncovered_settings(decisions, case). All settings were covered at the first attempt, because the worked example's decisions.yaml showed which patterns are needed.
insights.lesson: The early check is valuable (it costs seconds) but needs its own entry point.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.contract: add python -m cfdlib.contract --decisions cases/<name>/decisions.yaml <case dir> that only checks settings coverage; reference that exact command in SKILL.md stage 2.

insights.problem: monitor.preflight projects the full run time as (seconds per iteration) x end_time_full. For a steady run that stops on residualControl, the end time is only a safety cap (20 000 iterations here), so the projection is meaningless.
insights.diagnosis: The tool assumes a fixed run length (transient runs, or the linear Poiseuille case). Steady nonlinear runs stop when residuals reach a target; the useful projection is the number of iterations needed at the observed residual decay rate.
insights.fix: Case-local code in run.py fits the residual decay rate (decades per iteration) over the second half of the short run and extrapolates to the residual targets: 256 x 256 mesh, 0.054 s per iteration, projected about 3000 iterations (about 160 s).
insights.lesson: For steady runs, project from the convergence rate, not from the iteration cap.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.monitor.preflight: add an optional residual_targets argument that returns the decay rate per field and the projected iterations and time to reach the targets.

insights.problem: Pitfall 2 of the primer (GAMG with relTol 0.05 diverged) made it unclear whether GAMG with relTol 0.05 for p was safe here.
insights.diagnosis: The primer's pitfall was met in transient PISO (icoFoam), where every pressure solve within a time step must be accurate. In steady SIMPLEC the outer iterations remove the partial-solve error.
insights.fix: Kept GAMG relTol 0.05 and let the pre-flight decide: both meshes healthy, residuals falling steadily (x0.12 over the 300-iteration test on 256 x 256).
insights.lesson: The mandatory pre-flight turned an uncertain choice into a checked one in two minutes.
insights.guideline: openfoam-primer.md pitfall 2: say explicitly that it applies to transient PISO/PIMPLE final pressure solves, and that relTol 0.05-0.1 is the norm for steady SIMPLE(C).

insights.problem: With residual targets \(10^{-9}\) (U) and \(10^{-8}\) (p) the 128 x 128 run stopped after 2288 iterations, but the probed velocities still changed by \(3\times10^{-7}\,U\) over the last 10 % of iterations, failing the physical steadiness criterion (\(10^{-7}\,U\)) fixed beforehand. The coarser meshes passed or were marginal.
insights.diagnosis: SIMPLE converges more slowly on finer meshes (iterations grow roughly like \(N^2\): 211, 660, 2288 for N = 32, 64, 128), so a fixed normalised-residual target leaves a larger change per iteration on fine meshes. A 10 % window on a slow, geometric approach to convergence then shows a larger change. Normalised residuals do not translate into a known solution error.
insights.fix: Kept the physical criterion unchanged (no moving the goalposts after seeing results) and tightened the residual targets by one decade (U \(10^{-10}\), p \(10^{-9}\)). That fixed 32²–128², but the 256² run (9481 iterations, about 10 min) then missed the criterion again (\(1.4\times10^{-7}\,U\) over its last 948 iterations), so the targets were tightened by one more decade (U \(10^{-11}\), p \(10^{-10}\)) and every mesh was re-run with identical settings. Two re-runs of the finest mesh cost about 20 minutes of wall time.
insights.lesson: Choose residual targets from the physical criterion, not the other way round; expect each refinement to need roughly one more decade of residual for the same solution change (the change per iteration falls more slowly on finer meshes). Check the criterion on the coarse meshes and extrapolate BEFORE starting the expensive finest run.
insights.guideline: SKILL.md stage 4: for steady runs, state that the stopping rule should be a physical quantity (probe change over a window) and that residual targets must be checked against it per mesh; ideally a function-object-based stop (e.g. runTimeControl on probe values) so the stop itself is physical.

insights.problem: Stopping an outdated background run (the Claude Code background task) killed only the Python wrapper; simpleFoam kept running as an orphan and would have kept writing into the case directory the restarted run uses.
insights.diagnosis: cfdlib.foam.run starts the solver with start_new_session=True (so a timeout can kill its whole process group). Killing the parent therefore does not reach the solver.
insights.fix: Found the orphan with ps, confirmed its working directory with readlink /proc/PID/cwd, and killed that one PID before restarting.
insights.lesson: Background OpenFOAM runs outlive their wrapper; check for orphans before restarting a case.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.foam.run: write the solver PID to <case>/solver.pid and install a SIGTERM handler that kills the process group; add a foam.stop(case_dir) helper and mention it in environment.md ("Long runs").

insights.problem: The pre-flight projection for the 256 x 256 mesh (about 3000 iterations, from the residual decay in a 300-iteration test) was far too optimistic: the 128 x 128 mesh alone needed 2643 iterations, and iteration counts grew about 3.5x per refinement (239, 755, 2643).
insights.diagnosis: SIMPLE convergence is not geometric at one rate: the first few hundred iterations remove fast, local errors; the slow, cavity-wide modes dominate later and decay at a rate that falls roughly like \(1/N^2\). Extrapolating the early decay rate underestimates the run.
insights.fix: Used the measured iteration counts of the coarser production meshes to project the finest run instead (factor ~3.5 per refinement).
insights.lesson: For steady runs, run the coarse meshes first and extrapolate the iteration count across meshes; the short pre-flight is good for stability, not for run length.
insights.guideline: SKILL.md stage 3: "For steady solvers, the run-length projection from a short pre-flight is a lower bound; run the meshes coarse to fine and extrapolate iterations with mesh size before starting the finest."

insights.problem: Re-running the pre-flight after production would have deleted production cases: the worked example's build() renders pre-flight and production into the same N<N> directory (render_case deletes it first).
insights.diagnosis: Fine in a single sequential script (example), but not when pre-flight and production are separate commands that may be repeated.
insights.lesson: Give each stage its own run directory.
insights.guideline: Worked example run.py: use separate directories for pre-flight and production runs.

insights.problem: The mass-conservation check I fixed beforehand ("max |ψ| on the lid below \(10^{-4}\,UL\)") failed with my own stream function: about \(7\times10^{-4}\,UL\) on the 128 mesh, halving with each refinement, although the solver's continuity errors are \(\sim10^{-8}\).
insights.diagnosis: My ψ integrates face-averaged cell-centre velocities up each vertical grid line. OpenFOAM's face fluxes differ from that average by the Rhie–Chow pressure term, which is large only next to the singular top-right corner (all of the discrepancy sits in the last cell under the lid at \(x \to L\); in the interior the two agree to \(\sim10^{-7}\)). So the check measured a post-processing reconstruction error, not a mass error. OpenFOAM's streamFunction utility, built from the conservative fluxes, is exactly 0 on all four walls (and the same sign and scale as Ghia's ψ, in m²/s).
insights.fix: Use OpenFOAM's flux-based ψ for output (d) and keep my reconstruction as an independent cross-check of \(\psi_{\min}\). The mass check is redefined (after seeing data, stated openly in the report) as the net flow through the vertical centreline, \(\int_0^L u\,dy\), from the same centreline profile used for output (a), which is far from the corners. The original lid-residual number is still reported.
insights.lesson: A conservation check must use the conservative quantities (face fluxes), or be evaluated away from singularities; otherwise it tests the post-processing.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.foam: add read_point_field and a structured-grid helper (cells and points by (i, j) index for a single-block blockMesh), and note in the primer that postProcess -func streamFunction gives a flux-based ψ in m²/s, zero on walls, same sign as Ghia.

insights.problem: A scratch script named inspect.py crashed with "partially initialized module numpy".
insights.diagnosis: It shadowed the standard-library module inspect, which numpy imports, because Python puts the script's folder first on the path.
insights.lesson: Never name scratch scripts after standard-library modules (inspect, test, types, io...).
insights.guideline: environment.md: one-line warning; prefer running scratch code as modules with descriptive names.

insights.problem: The differences from Ghia did not shrink with refinement: for \(v\) near the downstream wall they grew from the 32² to the 128² mesh and levelled off at about \(0.009\,U\), above the \(0.005\,U\) pass tolerance I had set. The self-convergence of the simulation was clean (observed order about 2.1, finest-mesh uncertainty band about \(5\times10^{-4}\,U\)).
insights.diagnosis: Once the simulation is mesh-converged, the remaining difference is the benchmark's own error (a 129-point grid, printed to 4–5 digits) plus any systematic error of this simulation that refinement cannot remove. The coarse mesh agreed BETTER only by error cancellation. My tolerance assumed, without evidence, that the benchmark is accurate to \(0.005\,U\) everywhere.
insights.fix: Kept the pre-set rule (it gives WARN, not PASS). Added evidence instead of loosening it: a Richardson-extrapolated profile with its uncertainty band, and a sensitivity run with a different convection scheme to show that the converged answer does not depend on the scheme.
insights.lesson: With a benchmark, judge agreement against the benchmark's own accuracy, and test that the simulation's converged answer is robust (scheme, iteration error) before blaming either side. A coarse-mesh match can be luck.
insights.guideline: SKILL.md stage 5 / problem files: ask for (or estimate) the reference's own uncertainty and put it in the reference YAML; define benchmark tolerances as "extrapolated value within GCI band + reference uncertainty", and recommend a second independent benchmark when the first one disagrees beyond the mesh error.

insights.problem: My first draft referred to the velocity-profile figure as "Figure 3"; it is rendered as Figure 4.
insights.diagnosis: report.render numbers figures by section order (problem, theory, preflight, simulation, convergence, comparison), not in the order they are listed in results["figures"], and does not expose the numbers to the code that writes the text. Text written before rendering has to guess.
insights.fix: A case-local fig_no(key) repeats render's ordering rule (stable sort by contract.FIGURE_SECTIONS) and every figure reference is computed from it.
insights.lesson: Cross-references are numbers too: compute them.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.report: support a placeholder such as 4 in any text field, replaced by the figure number at render time (and have the contract fail on unknown keys).

insights.problem: The built-in browser cannot open local file:// pages, so the rendered report could not be looked at directly to check the figures.
insights.diagnosis: Environment limitation; figures are inline SVG strings inside the HTML.
insights.fix: A scratch wrapper patches plots.to_svg to also save each figure as a PNG, then runs the analysis; the PNGs were inspected (this caught cluttered log-axis tick labels on the mesh-study plot).
insights.lesson: Look at every figure before finalising; a cheap PNG dump is enough.
insights.guideline: cfdlib.plots: add an environment variable (e.g. CFD_FIG_PNG_DIR) that makes to_svg also write PNGs, and mention in SKILL.md stage 6 that figures must be inspected visually.

insights.problem: Nothing failed here; recorded because it worked first time thanks to the guidelines. The first full report.render call passed the contract with no errors, and decisions covered every OpenFOAM setting at the first check.
insights.diagnosis: The worked example's analyze.py is a complete, passing template of the results.json structure, and its decisions.yaml shows the needed setting patterns (e.g. 0/*/boundaryField/*, system/fvSchemes/divSchemes/*).
insights.fix: Copied the structure, not the numerics (the example is linear and uses no relaxation; this case needs SIMPLEC with relaxation 0.9).
insights.lesson: A complete worked example is worth more than a long specification; SKILL.md's warning "copy the structure, not the numerical settings" was the right emphasis.
insights.guideline: Keep the worked example passing and add a second one for a nonlinear steady benchmark case (this one), so agents can copy a residual-stopped, relaxed SIMPLE setup and a benchmark-style comparison.

insights.problem: Unclear how strictly "every number is computed by code" applies to free text that the agent writes in decisions.yaml and insights.yaml (e.g. "9481 iterations, about 10 min" in an insight, residual targets in a decision), and to hand-written cross-references and captions. A caption saying "the gap shrinks with each refinement" was also written before the final data and turned out FALSE.
insights.diagnosis: The contract checks structure, not provenance. Prose written early (decisions, captions) can go stale or contradict the data.
insights.fix: Captions and findings in analyze.py were rewritten so every quantitative statement is computed (figure numbers, contour spacing, tolerances, "settles rather than shrinks" with the measured numbers). Insights keep a few hand-written numbers as a historical log; decisions quote the settings themselves.
insights.lesson: Qualitative claims in captions ("shrinks", "agrees") are results too; compute them or condition them on the data.
insights.guideline: report-contract.md: state that decisions/insights are the only free-text fields allowed to contain typed numbers (as a log of settings and events), and that captions/findings must be generated from data; consider a contract warning when a caption contains digits not produced by tex_num.

figures.caption: The cavity, the boundary conditions and where each requested output is measured. Dashed lines: the two centrelines of the benchmark tables. The vortex is drawn around the benchmark centre; not to scale for the corner eddies.

Streamlines (lines of constant ψ) on the finest mesh (256×256). Solid: the clockwise primary vortex (ψ < 0, a contour every 0.01 UL). Dotted: the weak counter-rotating corner eddies (ψ > 0). The cross is the computed vortex centre, the circle the benchmark centre: they overlap at this scale. The centre sits right of x = L/2, the inertia effect predicted in Theory.

Output (a), (c). Left: horizontal velocity along the vertical centreline; lines are the simulations, dots the benchmark (Ghia Table I). Fluid near the lid moves with it (u > 0); lower down it returns (u < 0). Right: simulation minus benchmark at the table points, per mesh. The gaps do NOT shrink to zero: between the two finest meshes they change by at most \(3.4 \times 10^{-4}\,U\), while they reach \(0.005\,U\). They are not mesh error of this simulation (see the findings below Figure 6).

Output (b). Left: vertical velocity along the horizontal centreline (Ghia Table II as dots): fluid rises on the left (v > 0) and falls on the right, near the downstream wall. Right: simulation minus benchmark per mesh. Again the gap settles instead of vanishing: it changes by at most \(1.4 \times 10^{-4}\,U\) between the two finest meshes but reaches \(0.0092\,U\).

Iterative convergence. Left: residual of the u-equation per SIMPLE iteration; finer meshes need more iterations (the slow, cavity-wide error decays more slowly). Right: the physical check: how far the probed velocity near the return-flow minimum still is from its final value. It falls steadily to round-off level (the final plunge only reflects that the last value is the reference): the runs are converged far below the mesh error.

Mesh study, log–log. Left: change between consecutive meshes (self-convergence; plotted at the finer of the two); the dashed line has slope 2, the design order of the schemes. Right: distance from the benchmark. It falls with refinement and then levels off where the benchmark's own accuracy is reached: there the remaining difference is no longer an error of this simulation alone. The simulated ψ_min passes through the benchmark value on its way to the extrapolated value, so its difference first dips and then grows to a small constant offset.
